brief: Worked example of the Heard skill on SurveyMonkey's mobile apps. Segment: people who create surveys in the iOS and Android apps. Goal: rank which problems to validate next. Delivery cost, team capacity and strategy were not supplied and are treated as unknown. No internal data was used. Every verdict is a proposal awaiting a PM decision.
blind_spots: Only 1–3★ reviews were collected from both stores, so satisfied users and praise are absent by design.
Two source families, both mobile app stores. Web users, enterprise admins and review sites (G2 excluded by policy; Capterra, Reddit not collected) are missing.
Apple's feed gives no per-review link; App Store quotes link to the product's review listing (url_scope: product-fallback).
Records were collected on 2026-09-22 and imported for this report on 2026-11-13; recency is measured from the import date.
Records are anonymous reviews, not unique people. Theme counts overlap and must not be summed.
One reader made every clustering and intensity call; no second-rater agreement check was run.
SurveyMonkey runs no public ideas board, so there is no company channel to compare against.

themes.title: The response limit appears only after the survey is already out
themes.reasoning: The largest group, and the one that turns a pricing decision into a trust problem. The cap itself is defensible; finding it after respondents have answered is not, because the customer can no longer undo the send or choose another tool. The number is known when the survey is created, so it can be shown then and while responses arrive. The cap has moved over the years (100, 40, 25, 10), so the fix is the disclosure, not a particular number.
themes.beneficiary: Occasional creators on the free plan who name themselves: students, clubs, nonprofits, families, small businesses.
themes.cost: Unknown; requires engineering estimate. Disclosure copy is likely smaller than a pricing change, but nothing here estimates it.
themes.displaces: Unknown pending strategy brief. The visible trade-off is free-to-paid conversion that currently happens at the moment of lock.
themes.next_test: Show the cap at creation and at send to a free-user cohort. Proceed if surprise-paywall contacts and refund requests fall by a threshold agreed before launch, while free-to-paid conversion drops by less than an agreed limit.
themes.counterevidence: Several reviewers accept the limit and object only to learning it late, e.g. "I don’t have a problem with your 40 response limit" (S064) and "We don't mind paying for the service" (S177), so disclosure alone may not stop the complaints about price. Older reviews describe caps no longer in force. Collection kept 1–3★ reviews only, so free users who saw the limit and were fine are invisible.

quotes.text: When making the survey it never tells you this prior to completing it and sending it out.
At no point in the creation and sending process were we informed we would only be able to see the first 25 responses without paying $400.
I don’t have a problem with your 40 response limit, but I have a big problem with this being applied retroactively to surveys that were already running.

themes.title: Nothing between free and a hundred dollars a month
themes.reasoning: These are mostly not people refusing to pay. They are people with a one-off job who cannot find a plan shaped like it, and who leave for Google Forms rather than sign an annual contract for a single event. Several name the plan they would buy: per survey, per response band, or a cheaper monthly tier. That is a packaging change, not a product build.
themes.beneficiary: One-off and occasional creators who state their situation: students, small businesses, nonprofits, event organisers.
themes.cost: Unknown; requires pricing and billing estimate.
themes.displaces: Unknown pending strategy brief; a one-off plan could cannibalise Standard annual plans.
themes.next_test: Offer a single-survey or response-band price to users who hit the cap. Proceed if take-up and the resulting revenue beat the annual-plan conversions lost from the same cohort, using a margin fixed before the test.
themes.counterevidence: Price complaints come from free users of any paid tool, and several reviewers name a free alternative (Google Forms) they will use instead, so some of this group would not pay at any price. Willingness to pay is stated by only a few (e.g. S048). Nothing here shows the revenue at risk from a cheaper tier.

themes.title: People cannot get into the app or their account
themes.reasoning: Every one of these is a person who had already chosen SurveyMonkey and could not start. Unlike crashes, it is still being reported in 2025–2026. Verification email delivery and a blank "Not found" screen after login on Android come up repeatedly and are the threads to pull first.
themes.beneficiary: New and returning creators on iOS and Android, including paying subscribers (S216).
themes.cost: Unknown; requires engineering estimate and email-delivery diagnostics.
themes.next_test: Measure verification-email delivery and post-login error rates in internal telemetry. Treat as confirmed if failure rates exceed a threshold agreed in advance; a fix succeeds if the rate falls below it for two release cycles.
themes.counterevidence: Many reports date from 2014–2018 and may describe sign-in flows since replaced. Reviewers cannot tell their own spam filtering, SSO setup or device from a product fault. Several sign-in reviews are satisfied users with a mild annoyance (S143). No telemetry is available to size the failure rate.

themes.title: The app can show a survey but not work on it
themes.reasoning: Real and well evidenced, but most of these reviewers are existing customers with the web app available, so the cost is friction rather than lost business. The narrow version is worth scoping: individual responses loading blank and question editing account for most of it. Full parity with the web is not the ask.
themes.beneficiary: Existing creators and subscribers who check or edit surveys on mobile.
themes.cost: Unknown; requires engineering estimate per feature.
themes.next_test: Check mobile usage of the individual-response and edit screens and their error rates. Move to Build if blank-load errors affect more than an agreed share of sessions.
themes.counterevidence: Several reviewers use the web as a working fallback and stay as customers (S084, S114). Many reports are from 2014–2019 and may describe screens since rebuilt. Some items are requests (filters, dashboards), not breakages.

quotes.text: stick with the desktop version until they can build a real, fully functional app.
You tap on a respondent, the page downloads, but the page is blank.
Overall Survey Monkey is an amazing tool and I enjoy the service and plan to continue as a customer.

themes.title: Cancelling is harder than subscribing
themes.reasoning: Several reviewers describe repeated charges after an attempted cancellation, which is a regulatory exposure as much as a product complaint, and it lands on the same occasional customers the pricing theme is trying to win. A visible cancel path and a reminder before renewal are small, well-understood changes.
themes.beneficiary: Paying occasional users who bought one month or one term for a single project.
themes.cost: Unknown; requires billing and legal review.
themes.displaces: Unknown pending strategy brief; may reduce involuntary renewals revenue.
themes.next_test: Audit cancel-flow completion and post-cancel charge disputes. Proceed if disputes or chargebacks exceed an agreed rate, and judge the fix by that rate falling.
themes.counterevidence: Reviews are one side of a billing dispute. Some charges may be App Store or Google Play subscriptions the vendor cannot cancel directly. S189 describes a recurring charge for an ad blocker that may not be a SurveyMonkey product at all.

quotes.text: the auto renew option kept enabling itself after I disabled it.
I have canceled my subscription four years in a row!!  They keep charging me.
Paid for a one off month to get the most results, and then chose not to renew my account.

themes.title: The app crashes and takes the work with it
themes.reasoning: The evidence is real but old: most of these reviews are from 2014 to 2022, and the recency term pushes the theme down for that reason, not out of doubt about severity. The common detail is lost work. Watch it against current crash telemetry, which the company has and this corpus does not.
themes.next_test: Compare current crash-free session rate with the store-review trend. Move to Build if crash-free sessions fall below an agreed level.
themes.counterevidence: Almost no crash reports after 2022 in this corpus, which suggests the problem has been addressed. Device and OS details are rarely given.

quotes.text: After spending close to half an hour working on a survey, when I tried to run the survey, the app kept crashing and crashing.
Every time I would open the app it would crash, and not even bother to save my work.

themes.title: Support is a bot, a queue or a paid feature
themes.reasoning: Fewer reports, and support quality is not a roadmap item the way a paywall or cancel flow is. It earns a Watch because it compounds the other themes: the person locked out at login and the person double-charged both end up here. Most records in this theme are also counted under another theme.
themes.beneficiary: Paying subscribers and locked-out users who need a human answer.
themes.next_test: Measure time to first human response for billing and access tickets. Escalate if it exceeds an agreed limit.
themes.counterevidence: Small and overlapping: most of these records already count toward access or billing. Phone support limited to higher plans is a stated policy, not a defect.

quotes.text: support is suggesting it will take weeks to fix the problem they caused.
I have to upgrade my account just to be able to call customer support.

themes.title: People arrive expecting to be paid for taking surveys
themes.reasoning: A large group of reviewers are not survey creators. They want SurveyMonkey Rewards, the panel that pays people to answer surveys, or they followed a survey link and were told to install an app. The roadmap for the creator app should not chase this. It is kept as a theme, rather than excluded, so that its size is visible and does not silently inflate other counts.
themes.beneficiary: Not this product's users: Rewards panel members and survey respondents.
themes.cost: Not estimated; out of scope for the creator app.
themes.next_test: Check how many store installs come from survey-link install prompts. Revisit if that share is material.
themes.counterevidence: A slice of this group (S103, S120, S144, S203) are respondents sent a survey link who were pushed to install an app that cannot answer it. That is a real flow problem, and it may deserve a small fix even if the Rewards confusion does not.

quotes.text: I was directed to download this app, I did so thinking perhaps I needed it to complete the survey. NOPE.
i can’t seem to find where i can take surveys
I had over $20 in credits and they just disappeared.
